captions: Welcome to Camday.
This lesson was written by the Camday teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 1: Introducing Science.
Science is all around you, every single day.
In this lesson we will find out what science is, how scientists work,
how to stay safe in the laboratory, and how science changes our world.
We use electricity every day.
Being able to produce it is all thanks to science.
We also use thousands of materials.
Some are natural, like wood and cotton,
but many are synthetic materials developed by scientists.
Every kind of mechanical transport we use, from cars to planes,
was developed using science.
But our demand for electricity, materials and transport has damaged the Earth.
Global warming, the rise in Earth's average temperature, is causing climate change.
So here is a big question: can science help to reduce these problems?
Keep thinking about it as we go.
So what is science?
Science is the study of how things work.
How does pushing a switch make a lamp glow?
How does a heavy cargo ship float instead of sinking?
Why does bread dough rise?
How does a chick hatch from an egg?
And why does it get dark at night?
All of these phenomena, things we observe happening, can be explained by science.
Science has two main parts: what we have already found out,
and the processes we use to find out more.
Science is a very big subject,
so it is divided into different areas of study.
Physics is the study of energy, motion and forces.
Chemistry is the study of matter,
what things are made of and how they change.
Biology is the study of living things.
Astronomy is the study of space, including planets, moons and stars.
And meteorology is the study of the weather.
Each area asks different questions, but they all think scientifically.
Scientists work all around us.
Let's meet four of them,
and think about which area of science each one uses.
A forecaster tracks a typhoon with satellite pictures and computer models,
then warns people to stay safe.
This is meteorology.
An engineer measures how much electricity a solar panel makes in bright and dull light.
Energy and electricity belong to physics.
A medical researcher tests a new vaccine,
first on cells and then in careful trials with volunteers.
Living things belong to biology.
A chemist designs a plastic bottle that breaks down after use.
How materials are made and change is chemistry.
Real problems often need several areas of science working together.
Pause and decide: which area would study why the Moon looks different each night?
Science has been happening all around the world for thousands of years.
Hypatia of Alexandria invented a way to measure the density of liquids,
including blood and urine.
Ibn Sina set up the idea of collecting
evidence to check whether medical treatments really work.
Marie Curie worked on radioactivity, which led to X-rays and cancer treatments.
Rosalind Franklin used X-rays to help reveal the structure of DNA.
Har Gobind Khorana helped to work out how the body uses DNA.
And Feng Zhang helped develop ways to treat illness by changing a person's DNA.
Some scientists work alone and some work together,
but each discovery becomes a starting point for the next.
That is how our knowledge grows.

captions: To practise science well, we need the right attitudes.
Curiosity makes us want to find out how things work.
Perseverance means we keep going when things get difficult.
Open-mindedness means listening to other people's ideas,
and being co-operative means working well in a team.
Flexibility lets us change our plans when there is a better way.
Being objective and fair means accepting a result even if we don't like it.
Healthy scepticism means asking questions instead of believing everything we hear.
And integrity means always being truthful about our results.
Scientists work in a special way called scientific enquiry.
Let's follow an example about frozen ice pops.
It starts with an observation:
ice pops take longer to freeze than plain ice cubes.
This leads to a question:
why do ice pops take longer to freeze than water?
A hypothesis is an idea that might explain it:
the speed of freezing depends on how much sugar is dissolved.
From the hypothesis we make a prediction:
solutions with more sugar will take longer to freeze.
Then we test it with an investigation: five identical bags,
the same volume of liquid, different amounts of sugar,
all in the same freezer.
The bags with more sugar took longer to freeze.
The evidence supports the hypothesis, so we reach a conclusion.
If the results had not been as expected,
the hypothesis would need to change.
Science is a cycle!
A good hypothesis must be testable.
That means an experiment can support it or show it is wrong.
Plants grow faster under blue light than red light: this is testable.
We can grow plants under each colour and measure their heights.
Plants are happier under blue light: this is not testable,
because there is no way to measure a plant's happiness.
Testable hypotheses often link two variables.
A variable is anything that can change.
The independent variable is the one we change on purpose,
for example how long we heat some water.
The dependent variable is the one that changes as a result,
for example the temperature of the water.
That's why hypotheses often use the words depends on:
the temperature of the water depends on how long it is heated.
Scientists often use models to explain their ideas.
Models make difficult ideas easier to understand.
The particle model pictures matter as tiny particles.
In a solid they vibrate in place,
in a liquid they slide past each other,
and in a gas they move freely.
Models can be ideas we imagine, physical models we can touch,
or computer models. Computer models of the atmosphere are used to forecast the weather.
But remember: every model has limitations.
No model represents the real world completely.
To test a hypothesis, we make a prediction,
often using the words if and then.
If we heat the water for longer, then it will get hotter.
We must make sure only the independent variable can affect the result.
All the other variables, called control variables, are kept the same:
the volume of water, the beaker, the burner.
When only the independent variable changes, we call it a fair test.
Not every investigation is a fair test.
Some questions, like how an animal burrows into the ground,
are answered by careful observation.
Here is a real question from winter roads:
does salt make ice melt faster?
Predict: which beaker will have more water after ten minutes,
A with plain ice or B with salted ice?
Pause and decide.
Watch. One spoon of salt is sprinkled on the ice in beaker B.
Beaker A gets nothing.
After ten minutes, beaker B holds mostly water,
while beaker A is still mostly ice.
To make it a fair test, we kept the number of ice cubes,
the beakers, the room and the time the same.
Only the salt changed.
Explain what you saw.
The independent variable was the salt.
The dependent variable was how much ice melted.
Salt dissolves in the thin layer of water
on the ice and lowers its freezing point,
so the ice melts faster.
That is why salt is spread on icy roads.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Scientists use instruments to observe and measure: a thermometer for temperature,
a microscope or hand lens for tiny objects,
a telescope for faraway objects and a stopwatch for time.
A measurement is accurate when it is very close to the true value.
Scientists repeat measurements, and when the results are all close together they are precise.
Results can be precise but not accurate: they agree with each other,
but they are all far from the true value.
Accurate and precise results let us make conclusions we can be sure of.
Precise, repeatable results are also called reliable.
After collecting data, scientists analyse it by putting results
into a form that is easy to understand.
Huan is training for a 100 metre race and records his time for six races.
A table lists the results clearly.
A bar chart lets us compare the races at a glance.
A line graph shows the pattern, or trend, over time.
The pattern is clear: his time fell from 21 seconds to 15 seconds.
Huan is getting faster!
The conclusion is the final result of an investigation.
Huan's hypothesis was that race time depends on the amount of training.
What did we observe?
His time improved from 21 seconds to 15 seconds.
So the conclusion is: training leads to faster race times.
A good conclusion must answer the scientific question, be based on the results,
and support or disprove the hypothesis.
Now you can plan your own investigations.
Follow these five steps.
First, ask a question and make a hypothesis.
Second, identify the variables: which one will you change,
and which ones will you keep the same?
Third, decide what you will observe or measure,
and how you will record it.
Fourth, choose the materials and equipment you need.
Finally, decide how you will analyse your data to see if your hypothesis is correct.

captions: Experiments are a great way to learn,
but they can be dangerous if we are careless.
No eating, drinking or playing in the lab.
Wear safety goggles when using hazardous chemicals or heating.
And always read the instructions first.
Keep your work area clean and tidy,
check the label before using any substance, and when heating a test tube,
point the open end away from everyone.
Never taste anything unless your teacher allows it, report any damage,
spills or accidents, and wash your hands thoroughly after lab work.
Look carefully at four students in a laboratory.
Each one is taking a risk.
Can you spot what each should do instead?
Mai is lighting a Bunsen burner with her long hair loose.
Hair can catch fire, so she must tie it back.
Kim is drinking juice at the bench.
Chemicals could get into the drink,
so food and drink stay outside the lab.
Bao is heating a test tube that points at his friend.
Hot liquid can spit out,
so the open end must point away from everyone.
Lan finds a bottle with no label.
She must not use it, and should tell the teacher.
Which of these risks do you think is the most dangerous, and why?
Pause and decide before the video goes on.
Dangerous substances carry hazard symbols.
Always check the symbol before you use a substance.
Acutely toxic substances are poisonous from a single contact,
so never breathe them in or swallow them.
A moderate hazard causes harm if touched or breathed in.
Flammable substances catch fire easily, so keep them away from flames.
Corrosive substances, like strong acids and alkalis, destroy skin and other materials.
Substances hazardous to the environment must never be poured down the drain.
A health hazard can cause serious long-term damage, so avoid handling it.
In the lab we use scientific equipment called apparatus.
A test tube holds or heats small amounts of a substance.
A measuring cylinder measures the volume of a liquid accurately.
Beakers and conical flasks hold chemicals or collect liquids.
A Bunsen burner is used to heat substances.
Choose apparatus that is accurate enough for the job.
To measure 20 cubic centimetres of water,
a 50 cubic centimetre measuring cylinder is much
more accurate than a 500 cubic centimetre beaker.

captions: Isaac Newton made huge advances in maths, light and gravity.
He said he could see further by standing on the shoulders of giants.
He meant he built his ideas on the work of earlier scientists.
When scientists finish an investigation, they write reports to share their results.
Reports are peer reviewed: other scientists check the method and the conclusions,
so that others can use the results with confidence.
An important skill is to evaluate:
list the positive points and the negative points,
then make a judgement based on the evidence.
Science develops new knowledge.
Technology applies that knowledge to solve problems and make life easier.
Food technology helps farmers grow more, healthier crops.
Information and communications technology, or ICT, lets us communicate quickly.
Weather technology improves forecasts,
and medical technology improves how illnesses are diagnosed and treated.
Technology also helps science: computers let scientists work with huge amounts of data.
Here is technology in action: driverless vehicles.
Cameras and sensors track other cars, read traffic lights and watch for pedestrians.
Dubai plans for a quarter of its transport to be driverless by 2030.
Would you ride in one?
Science and technology bring many benefits, but they can also have negative effects.
Plastic is very useful, yet overusing it has polluted our planet.
Sometimes people misuse or abuse technology,
for example taking medicines for the wrong reasons, scamming people online, or cyber-bullying.
If you are ever cyber-bullied, tell a teacher,
a parent or another trusted adult.
Antibiotics cure infections that used to be deadly.
But if they are overused, bacteria can become resistant,
and the antibiotics stop working.
There is also a lot of biased information online.
Bias means telling only one side of the story.
Always ask who wrote it, whether they want to persuade you,
and whether other sources agree.
Modern life depends on electricity.
Burning fossil fuels like coal releases smoke and adds carbon dioxide to the air,
which traps heat and causes global warming.
Farmers use fertilisers and pesticides to grow more crops,
but too much of these chemicals can pollute the environment.
Plastic waste pollutes land and water,
and it harms living things in the oceans.
But science also helps solve these problems.
Solar panels and wind turbines generate electricity from the Sun and the wind,
so we burn less fossil fuel.
Scientists have measured carbon dioxide in the air on a mountain in Hawaii since 1958.
Here are the yearly averages.
In 1960 there were about 317 parts per million.
By 2020 there were about 414.
The line goes up every decade, and it gets steeper.
The amount is rising faster and faster.
This rise comes mostly from burning fossil fuels.
Predict: what might the value be in 2030?
Pause and use the graph.
Science and technology can solve many problems, but not all of them.
Scientists have found treatments for many diseases,
yet there is still no drug that completely prevents or cures cancer.
Science cannot stop natural disasters like floods, but it can reduce the damage,
with early warnings, flood barriers and stronger buildings.
So, back to our big question.
Can science help to reduce the problems created by electricity, transport and materials?
Think about what you have learned, and decide what you believe.
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: What is the difference between the independent and the dependent variable?
Pause the video now.
Answer: The independent variable is changed by us;
the dependent variable changes as a result.
Question 2: Is “plants are happier under blue light” a testable hypothesis?
Why? Pause the video now.
Answer: No – a plant's happiness cannot be measured.
Question 3: What does a flame hazard symbol mean?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Flammable – it catches fire easily, so keep it away from flames.
Question 4: What is peer review?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Other scientists check an investigation's method and conclusions.
